MetaTool Benchmark for Large Language Models: Deciding Whether to Use Tools and Which to Use

Every ReAct-style tool-use loop starts with a thought: do I even need a tool here? MetaTool is the first benchmark to score that decision on its own, separately from picking the right tool -- and finds that most open LLMs barely have it. Across 21,127 generated queries and eight models, only ChatGPT clears 70% F1 on tool-usage awareness zero-shot, and seven of eight models score under 10% at correctly declining to pick any tool when the right one isn't on the list.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Under the standard ReAct loop, an LLM acting as a tool-using agent goes through four stages: ① decide whether a tool is needed at all, ② pick which tool, ③ fill in the tool's input parameters, and ④ interpret the result. Prior benchmarks -- APIBank, GPT4Tool, APIBench, ToolLLM, ToolBench, ToolQA -- almost entirely target stages ③ and ④: given that a tool call is already warranted and a specific tool is already chosen, can the model use it correctly? MetaTool's own comparison table shows the gap precisely: of six prior benchmarks, only APIBank's evaluation range even lists stage ① (bundled into a single task alongside ③ and ④, not measured on its own), only APIBench touches reliability, only ToolLLM and ToolQA test multi-tool selection, and only ToolLLM varies scenarios -- none decompose ① and ② into first-class, separately-measured tasks the way MetaTool's four dedicated tasks do.

That gap matters because deployed agent frameworks like AutoGPT and MetaGPT depend on both judgments succeeding independently. A model that reflexively reaches for a calculator tool on "what's 7 × 9?" wastes latency and cost; one that answers "today's weather in Boston" from parametric memory confabulates. Testing stage ② in isolation is also harder than it looks: real tool catalogs are full of near-duplicate tools (two competing weather APIs, three PDF-summarizers), so a query that could be solved by more than one tool corrupts single-label accuracy unless the dataset resolves the overlap first -- something none of the prior tool-query datasets had done. MetaTool is built to close both gaps: a dataset engineered to have exactly one correct tool per query, and two dedicated task families -- awareness of tool usage, and tool selection under four different stress conditions -- evaluated across eight popular LLMs.

// how it works

The method

MetaTool has three pieces: the ToolE dataset, a test set for tool-usage awareness, and four sub-tasks for tool selection.

Building the ToolE dataset

The authors pulled 390 real tools (names + descriptions) from OpenAI's plugin store -- tools already installed in ChatGPT/GPT-4 and therefore realistic and widely used. For each tool, ChatGPT/GPT-4 generated user queries under four distinct prompting strategies: direct diverse generation (varied tone and detail), emotional generation (four emotions -- happiness, excitement, anger, depression -- baked into the prompt), keyword generation (extracting keywords from the tool description and writing a query around each), and details generation (elaborating on a direct-generation query). This produced 21,127 single- and multi-tool user queries, collectively called ToolE.

Because many of the 390 tools overlap in function (two weather tools, two PDF readers), a naively-generated query could be answered by more than one tool -- breaking the single-ground-truth-label assumption CSR depends on. The authors resolved this by embedding every tool description with text-embedding-ada-002, hierarchically clustering the tools, and manually merging or decomposing tools within a cluster until every query maps to exactly one label. Multi-tool queries were then generated on top of the deduplicated toolset: rather than exhaustively pairing all 390 tools, they took the 15 most "popular" tools (popularity = how many other tools it absorbed during merging) and generated 5 queries per pair, covering both tools used in parallel and tools used causally (one tool's output feeds the next). Every query -- single- and multi-tool -- was then manually checked by human annotators.

Task 1: awareness of tool usage

This is a binary "should I use a tool?" test. Positive examples (tool genuinely required) are a hand-validated subset of ToolE queries the LLMs themselves fail to answer well; negative examples are pulled in equal number from public instruction datasets covering downstream NLP tasks, common-sense QA (CommonsenseQA), and high-quality instructions (LIMA) -- queries an LLM can already answer without external help. The final test set holds 515 positive and 515 negative samples (1,030 total), scored with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1.

Task 2: tool selection, four ways

All four sub-tasks give the model a query and a candidate tool list L, and score with Correct Selection Rate (CSR) -- the fraction of queries where the model's chosen tool(s) match the ground truth (or, for sub-task 3, correctly match "none"):

CSR = 1|Y| Σy∈Y 𝟙[A(y) = ground truth] // A(y) is the tool(s) the model selects for output y; ground truth is t (task 1–2), ∅ (task 3), or a tool set Sₜ (task 4)
  • Sub-task 1 -- similar choices. The candidate list is the ground-truth tool plus its n−1 nearest neighbors by description-embedding cosine similarity, forcing the model to distinguish genuinely similar tools.
  • Sub-task 2 -- specific scenarios. Two variants: popularity-based lists of the top 5 / 10 / 15 most-merged tools, and group-based lists of the 10 tools most relevant to each of six occupations/personas (software engineer, elders, finance staff, house manager, artists & designers, students).
  • Sub-task 3 -- reliability. The correct tool is deliberately removed from the candidate list (along with its k nearest neighbors), so the honest answer is always "none" -- this directly probes hallucination and sycophancy.
  • Sub-task 4 -- multi-tool selection. The query requires two tools; the candidate list holds both plus distractors, and models are scored under a "choose 0–2" prompt and, separately, a "you must choose exactly two" prompt.

Experiments ran at temperature 0.0 across eight widely-used LLMs: ChatGPT, ChatGLM2 (6B), Llama2 (7b-chat, 13b-chat), Vicuna (7b, 13b, 33b), and Koala (13b). Sub-tasks 1 and 3 sampled 5 queries per tool (975 samples each); sub-task 2's popularity variant used 100/200/300 samples for top-5/10/15 and its scenario variant used 200 samples per occupation; sub-task 4 used the full multi-tool set. The first three sub-tasks were also run in a 5-shot setting.

// what they found

The results

Awareness is a two-tier problem. Zero-shot, only ChatGPT clears 70% on both accuracy (74.85%) and F1 (77.81%); every other model is well behind, with Llama2-13b's F1 bottoming out at just 11.53% (accuracy 51.94%, but recall only 6.21% -- it almost never flags a query as needing a tool). Five-shot prompting helps the weakest models a lot: Llama2-13b's F1 jumps by +42.79 points (to 54.32%) and Vicuna-7b's by +42.28 (to 55.71%), but ChatGPT stays on top at 79.71% accuracy / 81.87% F1.

Selecting among similar tools is merely hard; selecting honestly under distraction is where models collapse. On sub-task 1 (similar choices), zero-shot CSR ranges from Vicuna-7b's 73.46% down to Llama2-13b's 44.06% -- nearly a 30-point spread -- and five-shot prompting only compresses it to 72.94% (ChatGPT) vs. 49.85% (Llama2-13b), still a 23-point gap; the best five-shot gain anywhere in this sub-task is +6.58 points (Vicuna-33b), and Vicuna-7b actually gets worse under five-shot (73.46% → 63.67%, a −9.79 point drop). Sub-task 3 (reliability) is the real stress test: zero-shot CSR is under 10% for every model except ChatGPT (50.35%) -- Llama2-7b manages only 0.90%. Five-shot lifts ChatGPT to 78.49% but leaves the rest of the field mostly under 6%.

Multi-tool selection separates the field sharply, and models default to under-selecting. Under the "choose 0–2" prompt, ChatGPT's 2-correct-of-2 CSR (88.28%) beats ChatGLM2's (20.20%) by nearly 70 points. The dominant failure mode is stopping at one tool: Vicuna-33b selects only one (correct) tool in 48.49% of cases where two were needed. Forcing the model to output exactly two tools recovers much of that loss -- Vicuna-33b's CSR rises to 91.15% and Vicuna-7b's rises from 44.06% to 64.34% (+20.28 points) -- meaning the shortfall is often a prompt-following issue, not pure reasoning failure.

A 240-response human study (Table 14) makes the reliability gap concrete: humans hit 96% CSR at correctly saying "none" when the tool isn't available, versus an average of just 8.59% across the eight LLMs (best model 50.35%). Humans also beat every model on similar-choice and scenario selection, but interestingly fall short of the best LLM on multi-tool selection (66% vs. 88.28%) -- the one sub-task where models' facility with structured, multiple-choice-style output actually outperforms people.

Tool descriptions matter, and rewriting them is a double-edged sword. CSR rises as tool-description length increases (a fitted trend line across queries, Figure 7). Building on that, the authors had Llama2-70b and GPT-4 rewrite tool descriptions and re-ran all eight models.

GPT-4's rewrites help Vicuna-33b the most (+14.49 points) but hurt ChatGLM2 the most (−10.85 points); Llama2-70b's rewrites help Llama2-13b most (+7.83) but hurt Llama2-7b (−6.12) and Vicuna-33b (−4.37). The authors' takeaway for tool developers: pick a rewrite model matched to the downstream LLM -- there's no rewrite strategy that helps every model.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The core idea -- separating "should I use a tool" from "which tool" and stress-testing the latter under similarity, scenario shift, forced hallucination, and multi-tool conditions -- is a genuinely useful decomposition that most later tool-use benchmarks (τ-bench, ACEBench, RoTBench) still build on. But several parts of the evaluation limit how far the specific numbers should be trusted.

baselines

GPT-4 is used as a judge (deciding whether awareness-test queries are "genuinely hard") and as one of two rewrite models in the description-rewriting experiment, but it is never itself scored on any of the CSR/awareness tables -- an odd gap for a paper benchmarking "eight popular LLMs" in late 2023, when GPT-4 was already the reference point for the tool-use papers MetaTool cites (Gorilla, ToolLLM). More concretely, the paper's own text (Section 3.1 / Appendix C.1) states the roster is eight models including "Baichuan2 (13b)," yet every eight-column results table (Tables 2–5, Figures 4–5) lists ChatGPT, ChatGLM2, Llama2-7b, Llama2-13b, Vicuna-7b/13b/33b, and Koala-13b instead -- Baichuan2 never appears in a single reported result, and the discrepancy between the described and actual model roster is never reconciled in the text.

contamination

All 390 tools are drawn from OpenAI's live plugin store, meaning ChatGPT/GPT-4 (and quite plausibly the open Llama2/Vicuna checkpoints, via web-scraped pretraining data describing popular plugins) may have already seen these exact tool names and descriptions before the benchmark existed. No decontamination check is reported. Since the queries themselves are LLM-generated (via four templated prompting strategies) rather than logged from real users, the query distribution also reflects idiosyncrasies of ChatGPT/GPT-4's own generation style -- which could quietly favor models whose selection behavior aligns with that same generation style.

what's missed

CSR is a strict single-label match, and the paper's own answer-matching procedure (Appendix C.2) falls back to unspecified manual adjudication whenever more than two tool-name matches are found in a free-text response -- C.2 never says who does this adjudication or how many raters (the "two human experts" protocol the paper does describe, in Appendix B, is for labelling the awareness dataset's positive/negative samples, a separate step), and how often the C.2 fallback is triggered is never reported, which limits reproducibility of the exact percentages. The awareness test set (1,030 examples) and the similar-choice/reliability sub-tasks (975 samples each, 5 per tool) are also small enough that a handful of borderline items could move a model's headline CSR by more than a point, with no confidence intervals or repeated-sampling variance reported anywhere.

would raise confidence

Score GPT-4 (and newer frontier models) directly on all four selection sub-tasks and the awareness task rather than using it only as judge/rewriter; report the fraction of Appendix C.2's answer-matching cases that required manual adjudication and who performed it and how they agreed; re-run the reliability and awareness tests on a tool catalog assembled after each evaluated model's training cutoff to rule out memorized plugin descriptions; and reconcile the Baichuan2 discrepancy or drop the mention.

// bottom line

MetaTool's real contribution is the decomposition itself -- awareness and selection fail independently, and reliability (declining to hallucinate a tool) is a much harder failure mode than picking among genuinely similar options. That finding is robust across the eight-model comparison. The specific CSR values, though, rest on an LLM-generated, plugin-store-sourced dataset with modest per-condition sample sizes and an unreconciled gap between the paper's stated eight-model roster and its actual results tables, so they're best read as a directional ranking rather than a precise leaderboard.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. Tool-use awareness (should I use a tool?) and tool selection (which one?) are separate skills that fail independently -- zero-shot, only ChatGPT clears 70% F1 on awareness (77.81%), while Llama2-13b manages just 11.53%.
  2. Reliability is the sharpest failure mode of all: when the correct tool isn't even on the candidate list, seven of eight models score under 10% CSR at honestly answering "none" (average 8.59%, vs. 96% for humans), with ChatGPT the lone standout at 50.35% zero-shot.
  3. Longer, more detailed tool descriptions raise CSR, and a well-chosen rewrite model can add up to +14.49 points for one model -- but the same rewrite can cost another model −10.85 points, so there's no universally safe rewrite strategy for tool developers.
